harms.add: In Nepal's Tarai, measured heat at work was high, and starting earlier or changing clothing protected workers only in part.

sources.label: Pradhan et al., Industrial Health, 2013: climate change and heat stress responses in the Tarai region of Nepal

harms.add: Many more people feel heat illness than are diagnosed with it: among women garment workers in Phnom Penh, reports of symptoms such as thirst, heavy sweating and tiredness rose from 68% in cool months to 88% in hot months.

sources.label: Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025: heat stress among women garment workers in Cambodia, cool and hot months

harms.add: Losses differ by place and job: an ILO study of the Maldives estimates work lost to heat by sector and workload, as modelled estimates rather than measured wages.

sources.label: ILO, 2026: impacts of heat stress on jobs and productivity in the Maldives

harms.add: In Viet Nam, heatwave deaths from 2000 to 2018 rose more among older people and in the hotter south, and less in provinces that spent more on health or had more air conditioning.

sources.label: Nguyen et al., 2023: cold waves, heat waves and mortality in Viet Nam (Toulouse School of Economics record)

harms.add: Timor-Leste's 2026 WHO climate and health profile lists heat-related deaths and illness as not specified: an empty field, not a zero.

sources.label: WHO, 2026: climate change country profile, Timor-Leste

harms.add: A review of 76 studies in ASEAN countries finds air pollution changing how heat affects health, but not in the same way everywhere.

sources.label: Aung et al., 2026: heat-related health impacts in ASEAN countries, a scoping review

links: Where health services are stretched, more people die in the heat; in Viet Nam, provinces that spent more on health saw smaller effects.

levers.example: Timor-Leste's 2026 WHO climate and health profile shows heat-related deaths and illness as not specified, rather than as zero, which keeps the gap visible.

exampleSources.label: WHO, 2026: climate change country profile, Timor-Leste

atRisk.fact: Bhutan's 2015 WHO profile projects about 49 heat-related deaths per 100,000 people aged 65 or over by 2080 if emissions stay high. It is a projection, not a count.

source.label: WHO, 2015: climate and health country profile, Bhutan

atRisk.fact: Among women garment workers in Phnom Penh, reported heat symptoms rose from 68% in cool months to 88% in hot months.

source.label: Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025

questions.q: How well do national estimates of work lost to heat describe workers on the Maldives' outer islands?
questions.have: A national model with stated limits on local data and on assumptions about workers.
questions.could: Compare personal heat, rest time and output across matched workplaces on several islands.
questions.scale: Illustrative: about a hundred workers on six islands over one hot season

questions.q: Do heat symptoms and clinic visits differ between lowland, hill and highland settlements?
questions.have: Nepal has workplace measurements in the Tarai and studies of warming by altitude, but no linked comparison.
questions.could: Use the same sensors and symptom definitions across altitudes, linked to clinic records.
questions.scale: Illustrative: a dozen settlements across three altitudes over two hot seasons

questions.q: How many heat-related clinic visits can a linked reporting pilot find where national profiles leave the field empty?
questions.have: Timor-Leste's profile leaves heat-related deaths and illness unspecified, alongside an approved health adaptation plan.
questions.could: Pilot agreed case definitions, daily weather links and record checks in a few facilities.
questions.scale: Illustrative: four health facilities for six months
